In nineteen twenty-three, a German woman lit her stove with money.
Not to show off.
Because it was cheaper than firewood.
At the end of nineteen twenty-two, a loaf of bread in Berlin cost about one hundred and sixty marks.
By September, one and a half million.
By November, two hundred billion.
People carried their wages home in wheelbarrows.
Kids stacked bundles of cash like building blocks, and made kites out of banknotes.
Some families papered their walls with it.
Shops changed their prices several times a day.
Wait until tomorrow, and your money might only buy half a loaf.
But where did all that money come from?
You see, the government owed huge debts, so it did the easy thing.
It printed more money.
Presses ran day and night.
Think of a pizza.
Cut it into eight slices or eight hundred, it's still one pizza.
Germany kept cutting, and every slice got thinner.
Then, in November, they tried something almost funny.
Brand new money, with twelve zeros crossed out.
One trillion old marks became one new mark.
And it worked.
Because this time, they promised to do one thing.
Stop printing.
